content: The prevalence of depression among women diagnosed with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is significantly higher compared to women without PCOS. Research has indicated that women with PCOS are four times more likely to experience depression. Consequently, it is crucial to systematically assess the effectiveness and safety of antidepressant medications in this population. The objective of this review was to determine whether antidepressants are effective and safe for managing depression and other associated symptoms in women with PCOS. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and the Chinese National Knowledge Infrastructure. Additional searches were performed in trial registries such as the metaRegister of Controlled Trials, the National Institute of Health Clinical Trials register, and the World Health Organization International Trials Registry Platform. The search covered studies published up to June 2012. The inclusion criteria for this review were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that specifically evaluated the effectiveness and safety of antidepressants in women with PCOS. The methodological quality of the included trials was independently assessed by two reviewers. The risk of bias was evaluated across six domains: sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, completeness of outcome data, selective outcome reporting, and other potential sources of bias. The review did not identify any studies that reported on the primary outcomes of interest, which included depression and mood disorder scores, quality of life measures, and adverse events. Only one study met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 16 women with PCOS and compared the effects of sibutramine and fluoxetine. However, the study focused solely on endocrine and metabolic outcomes and did not provide information on whether the participants had psychological symptoms at baseline. Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the two treatment groups for any of the measured outcomes. In conclusion, there is currently no evidence to support the effectiveness or safety of antidepressants for treating depression or other symptoms in women with PCOS. Further high-quality research is needed to address this gap in knowledge.
